heading: How Florida defines a plumbing contractor

items.label: Definition
items.text: The statute defines a plumbing contractor as
items.quote: a contractor whose services are unlimited in the plumbing trade

items.label: No extra local license
items.text: A plumbing contractor may do this work
items.quote: without obtaining an additional local regulatory license, certificate, or registration: sanitary drainage or storm drainage facilities, water and sewer plants and substations, venting systems, public or private water supply systems, septic tanks, drainage and supply wells, swimming pool piping, irrigation systems, and solar heating water systems

items.label: Gas
items.quote: including the installation of water, natural gas, liquefied petroleum gas and related venting, and storm and sanitary sewer lines

items.label: Medical gas and fire lines
items.quote: air-piping, vacuum line piping, oxygen line piping, nitrous oxide piping, and all related medical gas systems; fire line standpipes and fire sprinklers if authorized by law

items.label: Other trades' work
items.text: Work belonging to another trade must be subcontracted:
items.quote: Such contractor shall subcontract, with a qualified contractor in the field concerned, all other work incidental to the work but which is specified as being the work of a trade other than that of a plumbing contractor.

originShared.text: Florida's Reciprocity form (DBPR CILB 32) covers applicants from Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina in General, Building, and Residential categories; it has no Plumbing category, so reciprocity is not available to plumbing contractors in Florida.
The route is DBPR CILB 10, Certification by Endorsement (Section 489.115(3), Florida Statutes), which lists Plumbing among its license categories.

Within CILB 10, the NASCLA-based Option A does not apply to this classification: the form restricts it to "General, Building, and Residential license" only. The route is Option C: hold a valid, current out-of-state license for at least 10 years, active now or within the last 2 years, of a license type "the same or similar as the license type being applied for".

Options A (substantially equivalent exam) and B (substantially equivalent licensing criteria) also exist, but CILB 10 warns that comparisons of state-specific tests are "very stringent and rarely approved".
For Option C, submit verification of licensure from your state showing at least 10 years and any disciplinary action, and a copy of your state's statutes or rules defining your license type.

Open question: CILB 10's 2-hour Florida Building Code course is required of General, Building, Residential, and Roofing Contractor applicants; Plumbing is not listed, and the document does not say whether Plumbing applicants face it.
